volumes.title: The Water Vole at Withy Bridge
volumes.text:
My name is Tobias Reedham. I kept the ferry below Emberwick for thirty-one years, and now that there is a bridge I have a punt called Patience and time on my hands. The librarian asked me to write down the beasts of the marsh. So this June I am poling from Withy Bridge to the sea sluice on the Grey Coast, twelve days, a beast a day.

The first found me before I had cast off. A water vole sat on the bank a yard away, eating a reed held in both paws, like a man with a stick of celery. Blunt nose, small ears, fur the brown of wet bark. Then it dropped in with a plop.

Out in the reeds a bittern was booming, like someone blowing across a jug. I have heard that bird every spring of my life and never once seen it.

volumes.title: The Grass Snake Swims
volumes.text:
Second day out from Withy Bridge, in the punt Patience, on the long ditch called Lazy Lode. I am Tobias Reedham, ferryman retired, writing a bestiary of the marsh one day at a time.

Mid-morning something came across the water ahead of me, drawing a neat V, with its head held up like a walking-stick handle. A grass snake, a good three feet long, olive green with a yellow collar. It swims as easily as an eel and hunts frogs and newts along the margins. It has no venom and no wish to meet anyone.

I picked one up years ago, off the ferry landing. It went limp, rolled over, let its tongue hang out and played dead most convincingly. It also made a smell I will not describe. I put it down and it recovered at once. Today I only raised my hat.

volumes.title: The Heron Stands
volumes.text:
Third day in the punt Patience, deep in the marsh now, with Emberwick's church tower gone behind the reeds. I, Tobias Reedham, stopped for my dinner at Alder Carr, where the herons nest.

There are nine great stick nests in the tops of the alders, used year after year and patched each spring. The young are nearly grown and stand about on the branches looking like disappointed clerks. They clatter their bills when a parent comes in.

The old birds fish the ditches. A heron's method is to stand. It stands in the shallows, grey and hunched, without moving a feather; then the neck shoots out and there is a fish crosswise in the bill. I timed one against my watch. Twenty-two minutes, one roach. After thirty-one years on a ferry I thought I knew about waiting. I did not.

volumes.title: Otter at First Light
volumes.text:
I woke before four on the fourth morning, moored in the punt Patience under Hollow Bank, in the middle of the marsh. Something was whistling on the water. I, Tobias Reedham, lay still under my blanket and watched over the side.

An otter and two cubs came down the channel in the grey light. She swam low, with only her flat head and a line of back showing. The cubs bobbed like corks and squeaked. She dived, leaving a chain of bubbles, and came up with a fish, which she ate on a mud bank, chewing with her head on one side.

Later I found their slide, a smooth wet groove down the bank, and a dropping left on a stone as a signpost. It smelt, oddly, of sweet hay. They were gone by sunrise. The bittern boomed as I lit the stove, unseen as ever.

volumes.title: The Eel Road
volumes.text:
On the fifth day of my punt journey through the marsh I tied up at Bess Tarrow's eel house, on the main channel of the Ember. Bess has caught eels here since she was a girl. I am Tobias Reedham, the old ferryman, and she gave me tea in exchange for news.

She showed me the last of this year's young eels going upstream. They are no longer than a finger and nearly clear as glass, and they climb her wet sluice boards by wriggling. They were hatched far out in the deep ocean, nobody knows quite where.

In the marsh they turn yellow-brown and grow for ten or twenty years. Then, one wet autumn night, they turn silver, stop eating, and go back down to the sea for good, crossing wet meadows if they must. Bess lets the big silver ones pass. They have, she says, an appointment.

volumes.title: The Marsh Harrier
volumes.text:
Sixth day, halfway between Withy Bridge and the sea, and the reed beds stretch to the edge of sight. I, Tobias Reedham, shipped the pole and let the punt Patience drift, because there was a hawk to watch.

The marsh harrier flies low and slow over the reeds with its wings held up in a shallow V, tilting like a tired kite. The hen is chocolate brown with a cream cap. The cock is smaller, with grey in his wings and black tips. Their nest is on the ground, somewhere in the thick of the reeds.

At noon he came in carrying something small. She rose from the reeds to meet him, and he let it fall. She rolled in the air, caught it in her feet and went back down to the young. It took two seconds. I applauded, alone in a punt, and felt no shame.

volumes.title: The Water Shrew
volumes.text:
On the seventh evening I moored the punt Patience at Clear Dyke, a spring-fed ditch in mid-marsh, where one can see the gravel bottom. I am Tobias Reedham, and I was only washing my kettle.

A small black creature ran down the bank, dived, and turned silver. It was a water shrew, no longer than my thumb, black velvet above and white below. Its fur traps air, so under water it shines like a bead of quicksilver. It nosed under stones along the bottom, bobbed up like a cork, and ate a shrimp on a leaf.

A shrew must eat every few hours or starve, so it is always in a hurry. This one hunted, ate, groomed and dived again four times while my kettle boiled. Its bite is said to numb a snail. I kept my fingers in the punt and wished it a good supper.

volumes.title: The Cuckoo's Lodging
volumes.text:
Eighth day in the reed beds of the lower marsh. I, Tobias Reedham, have poled the punt Patience past a hundred reed warblers and seen about six. They are small, plain, brown birds, and they sing from inside the reeds, a steady chattering like two pebbles knocked together.

The nest is the marvel. It is a deep cup woven round three or four reed stems, a foot above the water, so it sways with the reeds and rises as they grow. I found one by Sallow Reach with four eggs, greenish and blotched.

And one larger. A cuckoo had been there. Her chick will hatch first, tip the other eggs over the side, and be fed by the two warblers until it is three times their size and overflowing the cup. I looked for a long while, and decided that a bestiary records, and does not meddle.

volumes.title: The Harvest Mouse
volumes.text:
Ninth day. The marsh is drying toward its seaward edge, and the punt Patience now slides between banks of tall grass and sedge. I am Tobias Reedham, and today I nearly missed the smallest beast in the book.

A grass stem bent that had no reason to bend. Up it went a harvest mouse, the colour of a ripe wheat ear, with a white front. It weighs less than a copper penny. It climbed with its tail wrapped round the stem like a fifth hand, and let go with both forefeet to reach a seed.

Near by hung its nest, the first of the summer and still green: a ball of shredded grass blades the size of a small apple, woven on to living stems, with no door to be seen. The mouse pushes in and the wall closes behind. I have known worse carpentry on ferries.

volumes.title: Natterjacks in the Dunes
volumes.text:
On the tenth night I left the punt Patience at the marsh's edge and walked, because the noise made sleep impossible. Behind the sand dunes of the Grey Coast lie shallow pools, and from them came a churring chorus that carried a mile. I, Tobias Reedham, followed it with a lantern.

Natterjack toads. They are smaller than a common toad, with a thin yellow stripe down the back. Each male sat in the shallows with his throat blown out like a pale bubble, singing. They cannot hop much on those short legs; they run, and one ran over my boot.

They want pools that dry out by late summer, so that nothing lives there to eat the tadpoles, which must grow up in a hurry. It is a gamble with the weather every year. The whole chorus stopped when I sneezed, and began again when I apologised.

volumes.title: The Bittern at Last
volumes.text:
Eleventh day, in the last reed bed before the sea. For ten days in the punt Patience I, Tobias Reedham, had heard the bittern boom morning and evening, always from somewhere else. I had stopped expecting anything.

At dusk I was sitting quite still, splicing a rope, when a reed at the channel's edge turned out to have an eye. The bittern stood six yards off, a heron's stout cousin, streaked buff and brown and black exactly like dead reed. Seeing me, it stretched neck and bill straight up and froze. When the wind moved the reeds, it swayed with them.

We regarded each other for some minutes. Then it lowered its head, walked off between the stems on long green feet, and was gone without a sound. Sixty-three years I have waited for that. I wrote nothing down until morning, in case the pencil scratched.

volumes.title: The Sluice and the Seals
volumes.text:
On the twelfth day the punt Patience bumped against the timbers of the sea sluice, and the marsh was behind me. Beyond the gates the Ember runs out across the sands of the Grey Coast. I am Tobias Reedham, and I had run out of water to pole on.

I climbed the bank. On the bar lay some forty seals, curved like bananas with head and tail both lifted. They are not marsh beasts, but they are neighbours, and they wait off the sluice for the same silver eels that Bess Tarrow lets pass. One scratched its chin with a flipper and looked at me as at a late ferry.

So the bestiary is done: eleven days of marsh beasts, and the seals for good measure. I shall pole home against the stream, with nothing to write down. That will be a pleasure of its own.

volumes.title: Tracks in the Snow
volumes.text:
I am Nell Hathersage, the miller's daughter at Emberwick, and my bedroom is the loft over the grain store. From its window I can see the whole of Coppice Bank. These are my notes on the foxes that live there, begun in January and to be kept for one year.

Last night there was snow, and a fox was barking: three sharp yaps, a wait, then three more. Later came a long hoarse scream that brought Father out with a lantern. It was only a vixen answering. January is when foxes court.

This morning I followed the tracks. A dog's prints wander. A fox's run in one straight line, each hind foot set exactly in the mark of the front, like a row of stitches. Two lines crossed the mill field side by side and went into the wood together.

volumes.title: The Vixen Cleans House
volumes.text:
February on Coppice Bank, above Emberwick mill. From my loft window I, Nell Hathersage, have now seen both foxes by daylight. The dog fox is big and dark, with a walk as if he owned the wood, so I call him the Squire. The vixen is smaller and redder, with one white forefoot. She is Whitesock.

She has been digging. There is an old earth under the roots of a fallen beech, and every morning fresh soil has been thrown out in a fan at its mouth, and old bedding dragged clear. She is cleaning house.

I crept close at noon, upwind, and smelt them before I saw anything: a sharp musky smell, like the lion's cage at the travelling fair. Foxes mark their ground with it, on stones and tussocks, as plainly as we paint a name on a gate. I left no mark of my own.

volumes.title: Born Underground
volumes.text:
I, Nell Hathersage, have not seen Whitesock the vixen for twelve days. Her earth is under the fallen beech on Coppice Bank, in plain view of my loft window at Emberwick mill, and she does not come out. It is the middle of March. I think the cubs are born.

The Squire, her mate, tells me so. Each dusk he trots up the bank with something in his jaws, lays it at the mouth of the earth, and goes away. He never goes in. By morning it is gone.

Father says newborn cubs are blind and deaf, no bigger than moles, with short dark fur. They cannot keep warm alone, so the vixen stays curled round them for the first fortnight and her mate hunts for both. I had not thought of the Squire as dutiful before. He looks thinner, and rather pleased with himself.

volumes.title: Four at the Door
volumes.text:
The seventeenth of April, a warm evening. I was at my loft window over Emberwick mill with Father's spyglass when something small and dark tumbled out of the fox earth on Coppice Bank, sat down, and fell over. Then another. Then two more.

Four cubs. They are not red at all yet, but chocolate brown and woolly, with short blunt faces, small round ears and eyes of a cloudy blue. Their tails are thin as string. Whitesock, their mother, lay above them on the beech trunk with her chin on her white paw.

I, Nell Hathersage, named them within the hour. Bold walked straight to the edge of the bank and looked over. Shy would not leave the doorway. Scrap bit everybody's ears. Tuppence, the smallest, sat exactly where she was put. At a noise from the lane the vixen gave one low cough and all four were gone underground.

volumes.title: The Playground
volumes.text:
By the middle of May the ground outside the fox earth on Coppice Bank is trodden bare as a schoolyard. I, Nell Hathersage, watch it each evening from the mill loft at Emberwick, and it is better than any travelling show.

The four cubs are turning red from the face backwards, and their muzzles have grown long. Their eyes have changed from blue to amber. They stalk beetles, feathers, and one another's tails. Scrap has an old leather glove, heaven knows whose, which he carries everywhere. Bold pounces on it; Shy steals it when both are busy.

It is all practice. The crouch, the wriggle, the high jump with stiff forepaws: that is how a grown fox catches a vole in long grass. Whitesock brings them food now, and looks worn and thin. When the cubs mob her she simply steps up on the beech trunk, out of reach.

volumes.title: Worms and Beetles
volumes.text:
June, and the nights are short. The fox cubs of Coppice Bank are out before dark now, so I, Nell Hathersage, can watch them from the loft at Emberwick mill without the spyglass.

Whitesock, their mother, has begun taking them hunting, two at a time. I had imagined rabbits. The first lesson was worms. On damp evenings she leads them down to the mill pasture, where the earthworms lie out on the grass, and shows them how to listen, pinch one in the front teeth, and pull slowly so it does not snap. Tuppence is the best at it. Bold pulls too hard and sits down.

They eat beetles, crunching them like toast, and moths knocked down with a paw. Father says the hens are far safer than people believe, so long as the door is shut. Half of what a fox eats would fit in a teaspoon.

volumes.title: The Earth Stands Empty
volumes.text:
The fox earth under the fallen beech on Coppice Bank is empty. I, Nell Hathersage, watched it from the mill loft for four evenings in July and saw only a wren. The trodden yard is growing over with grass.

Nothing is wrong. Father says a fox family gives up its earth in summer, once the cubs are too big for it. They lie out above ground instead, in bracken or standing corn, wherever it is cool and hidden.

So I went looking. In the barley at the top of the mill field I found a flattened place the size of a cartwheel, with Scrap's leather glove in the middle. That evening five heads rose out of the corn one after another, ears first. Whitesock is in moult and looks as if moths had been at her. Her four cubs are leggy, three-quarters grown, and sleek as new pennies.

volumes.title: Dog Days
volumes.text:
August at Emberwick mill. The corn is whitening, and the foxes of Coppice Bank are hard to tell apart at a distance. I, Nell Hathersage, have had to learn them again.

The four cubs are nearly their mother's size. Bold is the biggest, with a white tip to his brush as long as my hand. Scrap has a nick in one ear from some quarrel. Shy is darker, like the Squire her father, and keeps to the hedge. Tuppence is still the smallest and stays close to Whitesock, who has the only white foot in the family.

They hunt alone now, mostly, and meet at dusk with a great deal of whining and tail-wagging, as dogs do. I watched Bold catch his first vole in the stubble: ears forward, a pause, then straight up in the air and down on his forepaws. He looked as surprised as the vole.

volumes.title: Blackberry Foxes
volumes.text:
September. The hedge along the mill lane at Emberwick is black with fruit, and I, Nell Hathersage, went out with a basket on Saturday to find the lower branches picked already.

It was the foxes of Coppice Bank. At dusk I watched Tuppence and her mother Whitesock working along the brambles, lifting their lips clear and nipping off the berries one at a time with their front teeth. Their droppings on the path are purple and full of pips. In the orchard they take windfall apples, and Father found Scrap asleep under the damson tree with a round stomach.

A fox in autumn eats what the season offers: fruit, beetles, mice from the stubble. Their new coats are coming in thick and bright for winter. The four cubs are six months old and look like foxes. I can no longer call them cubs with a straight face.

volumes.title: Bold Goes Away
volumes.text:
On the ninth of October I, Nell Hathersage, saw Bold for the last time. He stood at the top of Coppice Bank at first light, looked back once toward Emberwick mill, and went over the ridge toward the Northern Fells.

Father says it is the way of them. In autumn the young foxes leave to find ground of their own, the dog foxes first and farthest; some travel twenty miles. Scrap went a week later, squabbling with the Squire. Shy has moved across the river to the alder wood, where the ferryman's wife has seen her.

It is quiet at dusk now. I minded more than I expected, and said so. Father pointed out that I would not wish to live in the loft for ever. He is right, though I did not tell him. Tuppence, the smallest of the four, is still here at her mother's heel.

volumes.title: The One Who Stayed
volumes.text:
November, with frost on the mill pasture at Emberwick and the leaves down on Coppice Bank, so that from my loft I, Nell Hathersage, can see farther into the wood than at any time since March.

Three foxes remain: the Squire, Whitesock, and Tuppence, the smallest of this year's four cubs. A young vixen often stays on her mother's ground for a year, Father says, and helps with next spring's litter, carrying food and minding the cubs like an elder sister.

They are handsome now. The winter coat is deep and thick, red as a beech leaf, with black stockings and a full brush that a fox wraps over its nose when it sleeps. I watched Tuppence bury a mouse beside the gatepost, pushing the soil back with her nose. Foxes hide spare food against a hungry day. Two nights later she came back and dug it up, exactly.

volumes.title: Snow Again
volumes.text:
The last night of December. I, Nell Hathersage, am at the loft window over Emberwick mill with a blanket round me, and it is snowing on Coppice Bank as it did when I began these notes.

A fox barked an hour ago: three yaps, a wait, three more. That is the Squire. From the wood came the long hoarse answer that frightened us all last January and now only makes me smile. Whitesock has been at the old earth under the beech again; there is fresh sand at its mouth.

In the morning there will be tracks in a straight line across the mill field, and I will know whose they are. One year: two foxes, four cubs, three gone to their own ground and one stayed. I have filled this notebook to the last page, which is as it should be. Father has bought me another.

volumes.title: The Charge Against the Owls
volumes.text:
Paper the first, read to the Emberwick Field Club by Miss Verity Holloway, organist of this parish.

At our February meeting Mr. Crabbe stated that the white owls in the church belfry have been taking his pigeons, nine since Christmas, and proposed that the louvres be wired shut. I asked the Club to wait. I practise the organ late and have known those owls for eleven years. I have never seen either with a feather in its feet.

The barn owl is the white owl of our belfry: pale gold above, pure white below, with a heart-shaped face and dark eyes. It hunts at dusk, low over rough grass. I propose a fair trial. An owl coughs up the bones of everything it eats. From now until harvest I shall collect every pellet under the belfry and count what is in them. The owls, meanwhile, remain at liberty.

volumes.title: On Silent Flight
volumes.text:
Paper the second of Miss Verity Holloway, on the barn owls of Emberwick church, whose diet is under inquiry by this Club.

Members asked how so large a bird can fly unheard. I brought two feathers to the March meeting: a wing feather moulted by the belfry owl, and one from Mr. Crabbe's own pigeons. Swish the pigeon's through the air and it whistles. The owl's makes no sound.

Three things do it. The front edge of an owl's wing feather is toothed like a comb, which breaks up the rush of air. The rear edge is a soft fringe. The whole surface has a velvet pile, so feather slides on feather without a rustle. A vole does not hear the owl coming, and the owl, which hunts by ear, is not deafened by its own wings. The feathers were passed round. Mr. Crabbe stroked the owl's twice.

volumes.title: What a Pellet Holds
volumes.text:
Paper the third of Miss Verity Holloway, organist, being the first evidence in the matter of the belfry owls of Emberwick and Mr. Crabbe's pigeons.

An owl swallows small prey whole. Some hours later it brings up the fur and bones in a neat pellet, a dark, glossy lump about the size of my thumb, quite dry. They lie in heaps on the belfry floor. The verger has lent me a dustpan.

Soak a pellet in a saucer of warm water and tease it apart with two darning needles. The fur floats away and the bones remain: skulls, jaws, ribs like eyelashes. A vole's teeth are flat with a zigzag pattern. A shrew's are pointed and tipped with red. A mouse's are knobbly. My first twelve pellets held forty-one skulls: twenty-nine voles, nine shrews, three mice. No pigeon. Mr. Crabbe observed that it was early days. It is.

volumes.title: How an Owl Hears
volumes.text:
Paper the fourth of Miss Verity Holloway, read to the Emberwick Field Club in April, while the inquiry into the belfry owls continues.

A barn owl can catch a mouse in complete darkness. It hunts by ear alone, and the heart-shaped face is the instrument. It is a shallow dish of stiff feathers that gathers sound, as a hand does behind the ear, and passes it to ear openings hidden at the edge. These are not level: one sits a little higher than the other. A sound from below reaches them unequally, so the owl knows not only left from right but up from down. It turns its face until both ears agree, and then it is looking straight at the rustle.

As an organist I admire this greatly. I can tell when the tenors are flat. I cannot tell which tenor in the dark.

volumes.title: The Tawny in the Yew
volumes.text:
Paper the fifth of Miss Verity Holloway. The barn owls of Emberwick belfry are not our only owls, and in fairness to all parties I have examined the neighbours.

A pair of tawny owls lives in the old churchyard yew. The tawny is the brown owl, stout and round-headed, with black eyes, and it is the one that hoots. The famous call is in fact two birds. The hen says 'kee-wick'. The cock answers with a long wavering hoot. Heard together, they have been taken for one voice for centuries.

Tawnies nest early. By late April two grey, fluffy owlets were sitting out on a yew bough in daylight, as they do before they can fly. They need no rescuing; the parents are near. I gathered pellets from under the yew: wood mice, voles, a great many beetles, and one frog. They too are cleared of pigeons.

volumes.title: Five Eggs on the Floor
volumes.text:
Paper the sixth of Miss Verity Holloway, organist, reporting from the belfry of Emberwick church in the month of May.

The barn owls have laid. I climbed the ladder on the third of May, with the verger holding it, and found the hen sitting in the corner behind the tenor bell. There is no nest. She lays on the bare boards, on a soft bed of her own old pellets, trodden flat.

There are five eggs, white, rounder than a hen's and without gloss. They are laid two or three days apart, and she sits from the first. So they will hatch in the same order, days apart, and the brood will be a staircase of sizes. The cock feeds her on the nest. I counted a larder of six voles laid in a row beside her. Pigeons in the larder: none. Mr. Crabbe was absent with a cold.

volumes.title: The Little Owl by Day
volumes.text:
Paper the seventh of Miss Verity Holloway, read to the Emberwick Field Club in June, the belfry inquiry being now half complete.

Members who say they have never seen an owl should walk past Latchet Orchard at noon. On the wall, or on the leaning mulberry, sits a little owl. It is no taller than a thrush, grey-brown with white spots, and has fierce yellow eyes under flat white brows, which give it the look of a small cross schoolmaster. When watched it bobs up and down, then flies off low, in dips.

Its pellets are small and glitter. Under the wall I collected thirty, and they are made almost wholly of beetle wing-cases, blue-black and bronze, with earwig pincers and the bristles of worms. This owl could not lift a pigeon's egg. It is discharged without a stain.

volumes.title: Owlets in the Belfry
volumes.text:
Paper the eighth of Miss Verity Holloway, organist of Emberwick, on the family of barn owls above her head.

All five eggs hatched, between the twenty-fourth of May and the third of June. The eldest owlet is now a fat bag of white down with a long face; the youngest is half its size. They do not hoot. They snore, a long rasping snore for food that goes on all evening and can be heard in the nave. The choir has asked whether it is the bellows.

On Midsummer Night I sat in the ringing chamber from dusk to dawn with a slate. The cock came in fourteen times, and the hen, who has begun hunting again, five. Nineteen deliveries: sixteen voles, two shrews and a mouse. Each owlet swallows its vole whole, head first, and then looks astonished. Nothing with feathers was brought in.

volumes.title: The Owl of the Marsh
volumes.text:
Paper the ninth of Miss Verity Holloway. In July I left the belfry owls of Emberwick to their parents for a day and walked out along the marsh wall.

The short-eared owl hunts in daylight, over open ground. I watched one quarter the rough grass for an hour: long, narrow wings, a rowing flight, pale beneath with a dark patch at the bend of the wing. When it turned its head I saw yellow eyes ringed with black, as if it had not slept. It nests on the ground among the sedge.

The 'ears' are two short tufts of feather, usually laid flat. They have nothing to do with hearing. The true ears are at the sides of the face, as in every owl. It dropped into the grass twice and rose once with a vole. The marsh has no dovecotes, and I did not trouble it for pellets.

volumes.title: Leaving the Tower
volumes.text:
Paper the tenth of Miss Verity Holloway, organist, on the five young barn owls of Emberwick belfry, now nine weeks old and losing their down.

Since the last week of July they have been coming out on to the louvres at dusk, one by one, to exercise. They stand in a row and flap without letting go. They bob and weave their heads to judge a distance. The eldest stares at the weathercock for minutes together.

On the second of August she flew: a short, silent drop to the nave roof, where she landed in a heap and looked about to see who had noticed. By the tenth all five had made the journey to the yew and back. They still snore for food, and are still fed. I continue to sweep up pellets weekly. The count stands at two hundred and thirty-one. Mr. Crabbe reports a tenth pigeon missing.

volumes.title: Rain, and Mr. Crabbe's Pigeons
volumes.text:
Paper the eleventh of Miss Verity Holloway, read to the Emberwick Field Club in a wet August.

It rained for six days. This is hard on barn owls. Their soft plumage, so useful for silence, soaks through like a blanket, and rain drowns the small sounds they hunt by. The belfry family sat hunched and hungry.

On the seventh day the miller sent word. Would Mr. Crabbe kindly fetch his pigeons? Ten of them, wearing his own red rings, have been living under the mill roof, some since Christmas, growing fat on spilt grain and declining to go home. The miller's daughter, who watches foxes from her window, had counted them weeks ago. So no pigeon has been eaten by anything. Mr. Crabbe collected them in a basket and was very quiet. The pellet count will nonetheless be completed, for the sake of method.

volumes.title: The Verdict of the Pellets
volumes.text:
Twelfth and last paper of Miss Verity Holloway, organist, read to the Emberwick Field Club at its September meeting.

Between February and harvest I collected two hundred and ninety pellets from beneath the barn owls in the church belfry. They held the remains of nine hundred and eighty-six animals: field voles, 512; common shrews, 241; wood mice, 148; bank voles, 52; pygmy shrews, 21; young rats, 7; frogs, 3; sparrows, 2. Pigeons, none.

Our owls, then, are the best mousers in the parish. Mr. Crabbe has handsomely withdrawn his motion, and has built a nesting box for the tithe barn with his own hands. The five young owls left the tower this month to find barns of their own. The old pair roost behind the tenor bell as before. I heard them go out last night during the final hymn, or rather, I did not hear them.

volumes.title: Setting Out from Highgarth
volumes.text:
I am Ada Thornley, and I study animals that walk on their toenails. This October I have leave to travel with Jory Blackthwaite's drove: six score fell cattle, to be walked from Highgarth in the Northern Fells down to the autumn fair at Emberwick, twelve days by the green road. I mean to note every hoofed and horned beast on the way.

The cattle come first. They are small, black and shaggy, with horns that sweep out and up, a yard from tip to tip. A horn is a sheath, like a fingernail, grown over a core of bone. It is never shed, and grows all the animal's life.

Their hooves are cloven: two toes, each in its own hard shoe, which spread on soft ground and grip on rock. Jory counted them through the gate with a notched stick. His dog Tansy counted them again, to be sure.

volumes.title: The Fell Ponies
volumes.text:
Second day on the drove road from Highgarth to Emberwick. Our baggage rides on four fell ponies, and I, Ada Thornley, have walked behind them, studying their feet.

A pony does not have a cloven hoof. It stands on one toe to each leg, the middle one, and the hoof is that toe's nail grown thick enough to bear the whole animal. The cattle ahead of us go on two toes; the ponies on one. It is the first thing I look for in any track.

These ponies are black and brown, deep in the body, with long manes and feathered heels. They have never been shod. The stony fell wears the hoof down as fast as it grows. Jory Blackthwaite, the drover, says a fell pony never puts a foot wrong in a bog. I followed the bay mare's line across Mirk Moss and stayed dry.

volumes.title: The Hefted Sheep
volumes.text:
Third day of Jory Blackthwaite's cattle drove, crossing Hagg Moor in the Northern Fells. There are no walls up here, yet the sheep stay on their own ground. I, Ada Thornley, asked how.

They are hefted, said Jory. Each ewe learned her patch of fell from her mother, and will teach it to her lamb: where the shelter is, where the first grass comes. Sell the farm and the flock is sold with it, because the sheep know the hill and a new flock would not.

They are grey-fleeced and white-faced, and both sexes are horned. A ram's horns curl round beside his cheeks in a full turn. Each horn is ringed like a tree, a ridge for every winter when growth slowed. I counted six on an old ram who stood on a rock to watch a hundred and twenty cattle walk through his parlour. He did not approve.

volumes.title: Wild Goats on Kidstone Scar
volumes.text:
On the fourth day the drove road passes under Kidstone Scar, the last crag of the Northern Fells. Jory Blackthwaite the drover pointed with his stick. I, Ada Thornley, saw nothing; then a boulder got up and walked along a ledge no wider than a bookshelf.

Wild goats have lived on the scar longer than anyone can say, run off from farms generations ago. There were eleven. They are shaggy, grey and black and piebald, with beards, and the billies carry ridged horns that sweep back like scythes.

A goat's hoof is the secret of the ledge. The outer rim is hard and sharp and bites on rock; the sole inside is soft and grips like a thumb. The two toes work separately. The billy looked down at our cattle picking along the road, and I believe I have never been so thoroughly despised. The smell arrived a minute later.

volumes.title: The Roaring
volumes.text:
Fifth night out from Highgarth with Jory Blackthwaite's cattle, camped at the head of Stag Dale. Nobody slept. From dusk the hillsides roared, a deep, groaning bellow that the cattle answered uneasily. I, Ada Thornley, was delighted.

October is the red deer rut. At first light I watched a stag on the far slope, thick-necked and dark from wallowing in peat, with a dozen hinds below him. He roared with his head stretched out and his breath smoking. A second stag came down the ridge. They walked side by side for a while, stiff-legged, each measuring the other. Then the newcomer thought better of it and left.

That is how most challenges end. The roaring and the walk let each judge the other's size without a fight. The stag I watched had twelve points to his antlers. Jory's only remark was that he wished they would do it by day.

volumes.title: A Cast Antler
volumes.text:
Sixth day, coming down through the birches of Stag Dale behind Jory Blackthwaite's cattle. The dog Tansy brought me something from the bracken, and I, Ada Thornley, carried it the rest of the day: a red deer's antler, four points, grey with weather.

An antler is not a horn. A horn is a hollow sheath, kept for life. An antler is solid bone, and it falls off every spring. A new one grows through the summer under a skin of fur called velvet, faster than any other bone. By autumn the velvet is rubbed away and the antler is hard and ready for the rut. Only the stags have them.

This one had tooth marks along the beam. Deer gnaw their own cast antlers, and so do mice, for the lime in them. Nothing on the fell is wasted. Jory says it will make me a good coat peg.

volumes.title: Shoes for Cattle
volumes.text:
Seventh day. The green road from the Northern Fells ends at Garrow's Forge, and from here to Emberwick the way is stony lane. Jory Blackthwaite's cattle have soft feet. So for a day and a half the drove stood in the paddock, and I, Ada Thornley, watched six score cattle being shod.

A cow cannot wear a horseshoe. Her hoof is in two halves that move apart as she walks, so each half has its own iron plate, shaped like a comma: eight to a beast. Mrs. Garrow the smith nails them on while her son steadies the animal, and they finish one in the time it takes me to sharpen a pencil.

Nine hundred and sixty plates. The nails go only through the hard outer wall, which has no more feeling than a fingernail. The cattle minded the waiting more than the shoeing. So did Jory.

volumes.title: The Fallow Deer of Hollin Park
volumes.text:
Eighth day of the drove, and the first in the Lowlands. The lane runs for two miles along the paling of Hollin Park, and while Jory Blackthwaite walked his newly shod cattle past, I, Ada Thornley, walked with my nose between the bars.

Fallow deer, a herd of sixty under the oaks. They are smaller than the red deer of the fells, and prettier: chestnut dappled with white spots, with a black-edged white rump and a long tail that never stops flicking. Some are nearly black, and one doe was cream all over.

The bucks' antlers are like no other deer's. Above the first points they broaden into a flat blade, like an open hand with short fingers. It is their rut too. A buck stood under a chestnut making a noise between a groan and a belch, with great seriousness. The does went on eating acorns.

volumes.title: Pigs Among the Oaks
volumes.text:
Ninth day on the road with Jory Blackthwaite's drove. In Thicket Wood, half a day north of Emberwick, we met forty pigs walking the other way, in the charge of a boy with a horn. I, Ada Thornley, asked the cattle to wait.

In October the Lowland villages turn their pigs into the oak woods to fatten on fallen acorns. They were sandy and black-spotted, lop-eared, and wholly happy. A pig's foot is cloven like a cow's, with two smaller toes behind. No horns: instead the boars grow tusks, which are teeth that never stop growing.

The snout is the wonder, a tough disc with a nose's sense of smell and a spade's strength. One sow turned over a yard of leaf mould while I found the right page. Too many acorns are bad for ponies and cattle, Jory says, so the pigs do everyone a kindness.

volumes.title: Oxen at the Plough
volumes.text:
Tenth day. The Lowland fields along the lane to Emberwick are being ploughed for winter wheat, and at Long Furlong farm the plough was drawn by four red oxen. Jory Blackthwaite rested his drove at the gate. I, Ada Thornley, went in.

An ox is slower than a horse, and does not mind. These four leaned into the yoke and walked the furrow at the pace of a man thinking. Their horns are wide and upturned, tipped with brass knobs. The ploughboy called each by name, and each turned at its own.

At the headland they stood and chewed. Cattle, sheep, goats and deer all swallow their grass half chewed, bring it back up later, and chew it at leisure. It lets them eat fast in the open and digest in safety. The near ox chewed forty-one times, swallowed, and began on the next mouthful. I envied him.

volumes.title: Reading the Mud
volumes.text:
Eleventh evening. Jory Blackthwaite's drove is camped at Stanner Ford on the river Ember, one short day north of Emberwick, and the bank is a page of mud. I, Ada Thornley, read it before the light went.

Our cattle left paired half-moons, with the iron plates showing as a sharp edge. The ponies left single rounds. Between them ran the narrower prints of sheep. A neat little pair no longer than my thumb joint, the toes close together, was a roe deer come to drink at dawn. Deeper, with two extra dots behind each print, a pig.

Two toes or one: every hoofed beast I have met in eleven days is one or the other. Then Tansy the dog walked across the page, and I shut the notebook. Tomorrow the cattle are sold. I find I know several by face, which Jory warned me against on the first day.

volumes.title: The October Fair
volumes.text:
Twelfth day. Jory Blackthwaite's drove came into Emberwick by the mill bridge: six score black cattle from Highgarth, all present, iron-shod, with the dog Tansy at the rear. I, Ada Thornley, walked in behind them covered in dust.

The fair filled the green. There were Lowland cattle, penned sheep, ponies trotted up and down, a goat eating a notice. A horner had a stall of combs, spoons and lantern panes, made of cow horn heated soft, pressed flat and scraped thin enough to let light through. I bought a comb.

By noon Jory had sold the lot to a Lowland grazier with good water meadows, which pleased us both. He goes home tomorrow with the ponies. I have a red deer's antler, a horn comb and a full notebook, which the library has asked to keep. Eight kinds of hoofed beast, by my count, and twelve days well walked.
